name: active-categorical-perception
title: Active Categorical Perception (Beer 2003)
lead:
This is the iconic minimal-cognition model. A circle and a diamond are only
distinguishable through how their silhouettes sweep across the agent's sensor
fan as they fall; the agent must move to gather that information and then act
differently on the two categories. There is no symbol for "circle" anywhere in
the network — the category lives in the coupled dynamics.

at_a_glance.role: the agent catches circles and avoids diamonds from the seeded genome
behavioural categorization across object offsets + the generalization edge
how the coupled neural dynamics commit differently to the two categories

glossary.definition: Moving in order to generate the sensory information needed to perceive; here, sweeping to resolve a silhouette.
Responding to stimuli by discrete category (circle vs diamond) rather than by a continuous property.
A sensor returning the distance to the first object along a fixed direction; 7 are fanned ±30° about vertical.
Brain (CTRNN) + body (sensors/effectors) + environment (falling objects), coupled and run as one dynamical system.

biological_story:
Beer's agent is the simplest creature that can be said to perceive a category.
It lives on a line and looks upward through seven narrow rays. A circle and a
diamond falling toward it are, at any instant, just a pattern of seven distances
— and those patterns are nearly identical until the object is close and the
agent has moved to bring it across several rays. So the agent must act to
perceive: the early part of every trial, for both shapes, looks the same, a
small exploratory sweep. Only once the silhouette has been resolved does the
coupled system commit — sliding under a circle to catch it, or accelerating away
from a diamond. Nowhere in the five-neuron network is there a unit that means
"circle"; the category is a shape in the flow of the whole brain–body–environment
system, exactly the point of the minimal-cognition programme.
question:
Can an evolved CTRNN agent, embodied with a fan of ray distance sensors and a
horizontal effector, perceptually categorize falling objects by shape —
catching circles while avoiding diamonds — purely through the dynamics of its
coupled brain–body–environment system, with no internal "shape" label?
hypothesis:
A small CTRNN evolved against a catch-circle / avoid-diamond task will produce
category-appropriate behaviour across a range of object offsets: it will move
under circles (minimizing final horizontal distance) and move away from
diamonds (maximizing it), reproducing the active categorical perception of
Beer (2003). The categorization is a property of the whole BBE system — the
agent actively moves to perceive before it commits.

executive.what_is_this:
An evolved CTRNN agent (5 neurons, 7 ray sensors, a two-motor horizontal
effector) built on the shared brain, body and environment processes, tasked
with catching falling circles and avoiding falling diamonds. The genome was
evolved by the workspace's own genetic algorithm and is committed; the studies
replay it deterministically.
executive.verdict:
Reproduced. The evolved agent catches circles (mean final distance 0.15,
caught at every trained offset) and avoids diamonds (mean final distance 29.6)
— a clean categorical separation — within its trained offset range (±6). It
fails to avoid diamonds at the extreme untrained offset (±7–8), an honest
generalization boundary.
executive.verdict_detail:
From the committed seed (pop 80, gen 100, seed 0), verified in the test suite:
circles caught at all five training offsets; diamonds fled to ~25–40 units
across −8..+6; category distance gap > 8. The agent reproduces Beer's active
categorical perception. Two corrections were needed to make the task
well-posed: objects must be large enough to cast distinguishable sensor
shadows (size-1 circle and diamond are identical to the sensors), and the
fitness must be continuous (a plateaued reward traps evolution in a flee-both
strategy).

decisions_needed.question: Report the ±7–8 avoid-generalization failure as a boundary finding, or re-evolve with wider training offsets?
decisions_needed.context: Diamonds at offset ≥7 (beyond the ±6 training range) are caught, not avoided. Current framing reports it honestly as a generalization edge.

scientific_argument.main_claim:
Shape categorization in this agent is an emergent property of brain–body–
environment dynamics: the same sensorimotor loop yields opposite behaviours
for circles and diamonds, with no internal category representation.
evidence_for: Circles caught at all trained offsets (mean final distance 0.15 ≤ catch radius 1.5).
Diamonds avoided across −8..+6 (final distance 25–40 ≫ catch radius).
Trajectories share an early 'active perception' phase, then diverge by category (figures/trajectories.png).
Neuron-output and motor-neuron phase trajectories separate by category (figures/decision_dynamics.png).
evidence_against: At offset ≥7 (untrained) diamonds are caught, not avoided — categorization does not generalize to the sensor-fan edge.
key_figures: figures/trajectories.png — agent tracks circles, flees diamonds, at five offsets each
figures/categorization_map.png — final distance vs offset, circle vs diamond (the categorization plot)
figures/decision_dynamics.png — neuron outputs + motor-neuron phase trajectory, catch vs avoid
caveats: Objects sized 3.0 so circle and diamond are sensorially distinguishable (size 1 is not).
A single evolved genome; not a population of solutions. The behaviour is the strategy this seed found.

studies.name: cat-catch-and-avoid
studies.title: Catch Circles, Avoid Diamonds
studies.question:
Does the evolved agent catch falling circles and avoid falling diamonds from
the committed seeded genome, across the trained range of object offsets?

findings.summary: Clean catch/avoid: circle mean fd 0.15 (all caught), diamond mean fd 29.6.
findings.detail:
figures/trajectories.png shows the agent converging onto each circle's
position and fleeing each diamond. The early trajectory is shared across
shapes (active perception) before the system commits.

studies.claim:
The agent catches circles (mean final distance 0.15, caught at all offsets) and
avoids diamonds (mean final distance 29.6) — a category gap > 8.

derived.insight: Clean catch/avoid: circle mean fd 0.15 (all caught), diamond mean fd 29.6.

studies.name: cat-categorization-map
studies.title: Categorization Map & Generalization Edge
studies.question:
How does the agent's final distance to the object vary with the object's
horizontal offset, for circles vs diamonds — and does the categorization hold
beyond the trained offset range?

findings.summary: Two separated bands across −8..+6; diamond avoidance fails at offset ≥7 (generalization edge).
findings.detail:
figures/categorization_map.png: the circle band hugs 0 (below the catch
radius) everywhere; the diamond band sits at 25–40 across −8..+6 then drops
to ~0.5 at offset ≥7, where the object sits at the edge of the sensor fan
beyond the training distribution.

studies.claim:
Circles and diamonds form two separated bands across −8..+6 (catch vs avoid);
the separation collapses at offset ≥7 (untrained), an honest generalization edge.

derived.insight: Two separated bands across −8..+6; diamond avoidance fails at offset ≥7 (generalization edge).

studies.name: cat-decision-dynamics
studies.title: Decision Dynamics (Catch vs Avoid)
studies.question:
How do the CTRNN's internal dynamics differ when the agent commits to catching
a circle versus avoiding a diamond presented at the same offset?

findings.summary: Neural trajectories share an early phase then diverge by category; motor-neuron phase paths differ.
findings.detail:
figures/decision_dynamics.png (left) shows neuron outputs for circle vs
diamond overlapping early then separating; (right) the two motor neurons'
phase trajectory traces distinct loops for catch vs avoid.

studies.claim:
The coupled neural dynamics commit differently to the two categories: outputs
and the motor-neuron phase trajectory diverge after a shared initial phase.

derived.insight: Neural trajectories share an early phase then diverge by category; motor-neuron phase paths differ.
